articles.title: Amazon Is Ratcheting Up Its Fight With NYC Delivery Drivers
articles.author: Alex N. Press
articles.content_excerpt: New Yorkers opening Amazon’s app on Thursday were greeted with a warning: “NYC Council could add up to $5 per order.” A link invited them to “act now to protect low prices,” directing customers to contact their city council members about legislation that would require Amazon to directly employ its delivery drivers. Amazon rolled out the warnings, which also appear on packages delivered in the New York area, as part of its campaign against New York City’s Delivery Protection Act (DPA), which an Amazon-funded coalition has already spent upward of $8 million opposing. Amazon is warning customers that the legislation would put small delivery companies out of business, eliminate jobs, and delay their packages. articles.author: Branko Marcetic
articles.content_excerpt: Often, when people cheat on their spouses, they get kicked out of the house and strain their families. Not many can say they wiped out $1.8 trillion worth of share value and made the economy wobble. Yet this is exactly the case with ousted Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang and the scandal surrounding his various infidelities, including to a woman who is allegedly a Chinese spy. (Or is she?) The uncertainty around that question is part of the general murkiness of this entire affair (no pun intended), one tied into a knot of three separate political threads: the economy’s outsize reliance on the artificial intelligence industry, ruthless corporate anti-competition, and the simmering new Cold War with China. They demanded bold steps towards medicare for all, abolishing ICE, and an end to Israel’s genocide in Gaza. They trusted Democrats with the responsibility of ending corporate control over politics. No more corporate coronations. Democrats who enable genocide, ICE, and billionaire interests must be ousted. Call your elected officials and demand they reject the establishment and adopt an agenda for the working class. articles.title: What the Ottomans Tell Us About Plunder and Capitalism
articles.author: Y. Doğan Çetinkaya
articles.content_excerpt: Vivek Chibber’s recent interview on the Jacobin Radio podcast Confronting Capitalism and Vijay Prashad’s response in Monthly Review have reopened fundamental questions about capitalism’s origins, colonialism, and the transition from feudalism to capitalism in world history. Drawing on my research into Ottoman history, I want to make the case that societies beyond Europe belong in this history not simply for their contributions to the rise of capitalism in the West but for their own internal transformations. The origins of capitalism and its subsequent development through colonialism are distinct historical problems. articles.title: A Nobel Prize for Being Wrong
articles.author: Francesco Lamperti
articles.content_excerpt: The Nobel Prize in Economics isn’t mentioned in Alfred Nobel’s will. Rather, the gong was established in 1968 by Sweden’s central bank, which still funds it today. As Avner Offer and Gabriel Söderberg show in their book The Nobel Factor , this is no mere historical curiosity, for the prize’s origins can be understood against the backdrop of a conflict between Swedish social democracy and the champions of the market. Recognizing economists with the prestigious Nobel Prize was supposed to grant their theories the authority of the natural sciences such as physics and chemistry. Yet these imperfect theories do more than just describe the world: they help guide economic policy decisions that affect the lives of millions of people. articles.title: Reggio Emilia Stares Down an Uncertain Future
articles.author: Giulia Lasagni
articles.content_excerpt: From early morning on August 3, around a hundred people placed themselves between machinery and 45,000 square meters of abandoned land on the eastern outskirts of Reggio Emilia, a northern Italian city about forty miles from Bologna. They came to prevent more than two hundred mature trees, dense undergrowth, and a pond from being cleared for a Conad supermarket. The project also included other planned buildings as well as parking, pavements, and bike lanes. The occupation, reached by a small road off the Via Emilia, quickly became a permanent encampment, with a field kitchen, tents, and nightly assemblies. articles.title: Don’t Mourn Hakeem Jeffries’s Speakership. Organize.
articles.author: Austin Warrington
articles.content_excerpt: In the wake of the midterms, the entirety of left-liberal America was jubilant. Democrats won majorities in the House and Senate, outperforming even the most idealistic predictions. But it was not only the Democratic victories that shocked observers — it was the kind of candidates who won. Democratic socialists had their strongest showing of any election in recent history, winning 169 endorsed ballot measures and seats at the local, state, and federal levels — their strongest showing of any general election in recent history.
